title: Episode 132: Zachary Taylor and the Arsenic Mystery: The Sudden Death of Old Rough and Ready
description:
On July fourth, eighteen fifty, President Zachary Taylor attended hours of scorching, suffocating Independence Day ceremonies at the base of the unfinished Washington Monument. Temperatures soared into the nineties, and the sixty-five-year-old President was parched and exhausted. Returning to the Executive Mansion, Taylor consumed copious amounts of raw cherries, cucumbers, and iced milk to quench his thirst. Within hours, he fell violently ill with severe abdominal cramps, violent vomiting, and dehydrating diarrhea, diagnosed by his doctors as 'cholera morbus.' Five days later, on July ninth, eighteen fifty, Old Rough and Ready was dead.

Taylor's sudden death dramatically altered American history. His demise removed the single greatest obstacle to the Compromise of eighteen fifty: his successor, Millard Fillmore, immediately signed the compromise bills into law, including the despised Fugitive Slave Act. Almost immediately, dark rumors circulated: had the President truly died of cherries and milk, or had he been assassinated by pro-slavery conspirators who slipped arsenic into his food to eliminate an unyielding nationalist leader?

For over a century, the assassination theory lingered in American folklore. Finally, in June nineteen ninety-one, at the urging of a prominent historian and with the consent of Taylor's descendants, federal authorities exhumed the body of the twelfth President from his family crypt in Louisville, Kentucky. Forensic pathologists and nuclear scientists analyzed hair and nail samples using neutron activation analysis to test for poison. Join George as he unravels the medical, political, and forensic truth behind the death of Zachary Taylor.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our exploration of President Zachary Taylor with one of the most enduring historical mysteries of the American presidency: the death of Old Rough and Ready. In July eighteen fifty, at the height of a national crisis that threatened civil war, President Taylor died suddenly after eating a bowl of cherries and iced milk. His death paved the way for the Compromise of eighteen fifty and raised suspicions of murder that lasted for over a century—leading to the unprecedented exhumation of a president in nineteen ninety-one. Here is George with the full, fascinating investigation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: SCORCHING SUN AT THE WASHINGTON MONUMENT
The fourth of July, eighteen fifty, was one of the most sweltering, oppressive summer days in the history of the nation's capital. The humidity off the Potomac River was suffocating, and temperatures in Washington soared into the high nineties under a blazing, cloudless sun. Despite the brutal heat, President Zachary Taylor felt a deep duty to attend the grand Independence Day ceremonies held at the base of the unfinished Washington Monument.
For more than three hours, the sixty-five-year-old President sat on an open wooden platform in the baking sun, listening to hours of bombastic patriotic oratory from Senator Henry Foote of Mississippi and other dignitaries. Taylor was parched, exhausted, and visibly sweating through his black suit. To cool himself, he drank several glasses of cold water from local street pumps.
Returning to the Executive Mansion around four in the afternoon, Taylor was desperately thirsty and famished. Calling for refreshments, he was served a large silver bowl of fresh, raw black cherries, accompanied by large pitchers of iced whole milk and sliced garden cucumbers. Taylor devoured the cherries and drank pitcher after pitcher of cold milk, laughing with his family that nothing on Earth tasted better on a hot summer day. It was the last peaceful meal Old Rough and Ready would ever enjoy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE AGONY IN THE WHITE HOUSE
Around eight o'clock that evening, President Taylor was seized with violent, agonizing abdominal cramps. Within hours, he was wracked by violent vomiting and severe dehydrating diarrhea. The White House physician, Dr. Alexander Wotherspoon, was summoned in the middle of the night and diagnosed the President with 'cholera morbus'—a nineteenth-century term used to describe acute, severe gastroenteritis.
Over the next three days, Taylor's condition deteriorated rapidly. The President was running a high fever, his body was severely dehydrated, and his pulse grew weak and thready. As was common in mid-nineteenth-century medicine, a team of prominent consulting physicians subjected the weakened President to aggressive, counterproductive treatments. They administered heavy doses of calomel—a toxic mercury compound—along with opium, ipecac to induce vomiting, quinine, and bled him with live leeches applied to his skin.
The treatments devastated Taylor's remaining strength, destroying his intestinal lining and sending his body into toxic shock. Modern medical experts who have examined the historical case notes believe that the massive doses of calomel and the bloodletting actively accelerated the President's death, turning a manageable bacterial infection into a lethal cascade of organ failure. By July eighth, typhus-like fever and secondary peritonitis had set in, and the President slipped into periods of deep delirium. Outside the Executive Mansion, thousands of citizens gathered in silence, holding prayer vigils under the trees of Lafayette Square as church bells tolled across the city.
Recognizing that his earthly end was near, the old soldier remained calm, stoic, and dignified. Surrounding his bedside were his distraught wife Margaret, who had warned him that the presidency would cost him his life, his beloved daughter, his weeping cabinet secretaries, and his old friend, Vice President Millard Fillmore. Gathering his final, labored breath, Taylor whispered his last words to the republic he had served for forty years: 'I am about to die. I expect the summons soon. I have endeavored to do my duty. I have no regret, but I am sorry that I am about to leave my friends.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MIDNIGHT PASSING OF A PRESIDENT
At thirty-five minutes past ten o'clock on the evening of Tuesday, July ninth, eighteen fifty, Zachary Taylor drew his last breath. He had served as President of the United States for exactly sixteen months and four days. Outside the White House, a crowd of hundreds of citizens stood in silent shock in the dark gardens as the lights in the presidential suite were extinguished.
On July thirteenth, Washington came to a standstill for a colossal military funeral. Thousands of soldiers, diplomats, and citizens lined Pennsylvania Avenue as Taylor's casket, draped in the American flag, was carried on a black funeral car pulled by eight white horses. Walking directly behind the hearse, with his head bowed and his master's empty boots reversed in the stirrups of his saddle, was Taylor's beloved white warhorse, Old Whitey. Spectators wept as the faithful steed walked the dusty streets of Washington.
Taylor was temporarily interred in the Congressional Cemetery in Washington before being transported home to Louisville, Kentucky, where he was laid to rest in his family's limestone crypt at Springfield Plantation. The nation mourned a rugged hero. But in the corridors of power, Taylor's death produced an immediate, seismic political earthquake.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE POLITICAL REVERSAL OF 1850
The death of Zachary Taylor dramatically transformed the course of American history. Had Taylor lived, he was fully prepared to veto Henry Clay's omnibus compromise bill and use military force to admit California as a free state without concessions to the South. Taylor's sudden demise removed the single greatest obstacle to compromise.
Vice President Millard Fillmore, who succeeded to the presidency the following morning, took an entirely different approach. A moderate Northern Whig from New York, Fillmore believed that compromise was essential to save the Union from immediate civil war. Fillmore accepted the resignations of Taylor's anti-compromise cabinet and replaced them with statesmen who favored compromise, appointing Daniel Webster as Secretary of State.
Working with Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois, Fillmore threw the full weight of the presidency behind the compromise. Douglas cleverly broke Clay's giant omnibus bill into five separate legislative measures, allowing different coalitions of Northern and Southern members to pass each one. In September eighteen fifty, Fillmore signed all five bills into law, establishing the Compromise of eighteen fifty.
California was admitted as a free state; New Mexico and Utah were organized as territories without restrictions on slavery; the slave trade was abolished in Washington, D.C.; Texas surrendered its claims to New Mexico in exchange for ten million dollars; and Congress enacted the notorious, draconian Fugitive Slave Act. The compromise avoided civil war for ten years, but it set the nation on an irreconcilable path toward the bloodbath of eighteen sixty-one.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE POISON CONSPIRACY
Almost from the moment Zachary Taylor drew his last breath, dark whispers of foul play circulated through the boarding houses and political taverns of Washington. To many contemporaries, the timing was simply too convenient, too miraculous for the pro-slavery faction, to be a mere accident of nature. Here was an iron-willed military President standing directly in the path of Southern territorial ambitions—a man who had threatened to hang secessionists as traitors and pledged to veto the South's cherished compromise measures with the full power of his office. Suddenly, following a single Fourth of July meal, the immovable obstacle was dead, replaced by a pliant successor who immediately signed every Southern concession into law.
Southern firebrands like Robert Toombs and Alexander Stephens had openly rejoiced at the news, with some Southern newspapers bluntly describing Taylor's sudden demise as a providential deliverance for the South. Abolitionists across the North, meanwhile, began openly accusing Southern conspirators of political assassination. Whispers spread that the cherries, the milk, or the ice had been laced with poison by an operative within the White House kitchen staff.
Over the decades, historians and conspiracy theorists pointed out suspicious circumstances. The symptoms Taylor exhibited—sudden acute abdominal pain, severe vomiting, burning throat, fever, and rapid circulatory collapse—were virtually identical to the classic clinical symptoms of acute arsenic poisoning. Arsenic was readily available in the nineteenth century as a tasteless, odorless white powder, commonly used as rat poison and easily slipped into milk or cherries.
In the late twentieth century, the theory gained explosive new life through the research of Clara Rising, a former humanities professor at the University of Florida. Rising spent years analyzing contemporary medical records, letters, and diaries. She argued that radical Southern secessionists—or political operatives seeking to save the Union through compromise—had systematically poisoned the President to remove an unyielding obstacle. Rising convinced Taylor's living descendants, including his great-great-great-grandson, to seek a scientific resolution to the century-old mystery.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE EXHUMATION OF A PRESIDENT: JUNE 1991
In June nineteen ninety-one, federal and Kentucky state authorities made history. With court permission, the coroner of Jefferson County, Kentucky, ordered the exhumation of the twelfth President of the United States. It was the first and only time in American history that the body of a United States President was disinterred specifically to conduct a forensic homicide investigation.
At dawn on June seventeenth, nineteen ninety-one, a team of forensic scientists, medical examiners, and cemetery workers gathered at the Zachary Taylor National Cemetery in Louisville. Working with solemn reverence, they lifted the heavy marble slab of the family mausoleum and removed the President's ornate cast-iron casket. The casket was transported under police escort to the state medical examiner's office in Louisville.
Dr. George Nichols, the chief medical examiner of Kentucky, opened the casket alongside renowned forensic pathologist Dr. William Maples. Because Taylor had been interred in an airtight, hermetically sealed metallic coffin, his remains were remarkably well preserved. Forensic pathologists meticulously harvested samples of hair, fingernails, bone, and mummified tissue. The samples were immediately flown to the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee and the Center for Trace Element Analysis for advanced nuclear testing using neutron activation analysis—a state-of-the-art technology capable of detecting trace elements down to parts per billion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SCIENTIFIC VERDICT
Nine days later, on June twenty-sixth, nineteen ninety-one, Dr. George Nichols held a packed national press conference in Louisville to announce the definitive scientific findings. The verdict was clear, undeniable, and conclusive: Zachary Taylor was not poisoned.
The neutron activation analysis revealed trace amounts of arsenic in Taylor's hair and nails, but at levels hundreds of times lower than a lethal dose. The trace amounts were entirely consistent with natural background levels present in nineteenth-century food, water, and patent medicines. Pathologists concluded that Taylor had died of acute gastroenteritis, complicated by severe dehydration and heat exhaustion, exacerbated by contaminated water and the bleeding and toxic calomel administered by his well-meaning physicians.
The cherries and iced milk were not poisoned with arsenic, but they were almost certainly contaminated with lethal bacteria. In eighteen fifty, Washington had no modern sewer system. Raw sewage from outdoor privies seeped into the shallow groundwater and contaminated the city's water pumps. The unpasteurized milk and raw fruit Taylor consumed were breeding grounds for cholera, salmonella, or amoebic dysentery.
Zachary Taylor was re-interred in his Louisville tomb with full military honors. The forensic investigation demolished a century of assassination rumors, proving that Old Rough and Ready was brought down not by a traitor's vial of poison, but by the deadly, primitive sanitation of the city he had sworn to defend.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The forensic exhumation of Zachary Taylor solved one of the great mysteries of the American presidency, proving that nature, contaminated water, and nineteenth-century medicine were responsible for his tragic death. Next week, we meet the man who inherited his office: America's thirteenth President, Millard Fillmore—born in a humble log cabin, who signed the Compromise of eighteen fifty and preserved the Union for another decade. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
